newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's stubborn peso suggests trouble ahead.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's stubborn peso suggests trouble ahead.

text.p: The persistent strength of the Mexican peso three weeks ahead of key elections is baffling economists who wonder how long the buoyancy can last, or whether they should brace themselves for a sudden crunch.

Last week Finance Ministry officials suggested there was room for the peso to ease and that the adjustment was unlikely to be smooth. The peso is trading at 7.95 to the dollar when markets had expected it to be well over 8.0 by now.

Market players in Mexico and abroad agree the currency is overvalued, but disagree on the size and timing of any depreciation. Peso futures contracts traded in Chicago show investors are hedging against a depreciation.

"We expected to see weakness in the peso in the run up to the elections and we still may, but there are no signs of it at this stage," said Chip Brown, senior economist for Latin America at Morgan Stanley, adding that it was a moot point when any adjustment might come.
"You could make an equal case for a week before or a week after the election," he said.
By Brown's calculations the peso is overvalued by about nine percent, but he said he would not be unduly worried until overvaluation reached around 15 percent.

But Gray Newman, chief economist for Mexico at HSBC James Capel here, said the peso's failure to adjust now was storing up problems longer term and said he was expecting a peso correction later this year.
"The current level of the peso is not a reason for concern, what is is the strength with which it has appreciated since December 1995," Newman said.

"While we're unlikely to have an event risk between now and the election, we will have one later in the year," he said, adding this was likely to happen around September when people realized the currency was well off year-end targets.
Newman set his year-end target at 8.9 pesos to the dollar a year ago and was revising it to 8.4 or 8.5.

Brown had been forecasting nine pesos to the dollar by year end and is also weighing a revision and two weeks ago a central bank survey of independent economists showed average expectations of a year-end level of 8.64 to the dollar.
The peso's strength has been helped by a sharp rise in interest rates at last week's auction of 28-day government paper, just when the currency showed signs of weakening.

Some market players scent foul play in the run-up to the July 6 mid-term poll. With the ruling PRI in danger of losing its 68-year majority in Congress, they suspect the government is keen to keep a strong peso at least until election day.

A steep 113 basis point increase in the rate for the bellwether 28-day Cetes at the central bank's auction on Tuesday sent the benchmark 48-hour peso up 1.2 percent and the strength has continued since then.
But a central bank official firmly denied the bank had any policy other than meeting market demand.
"The Bank of Mexico does not have an interest rate target, it has a quantity target which is to satisfy demand for the monetary base," he said.

The Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME), where traders hedge bets on currency moves, has seen abnormally high two-way volumes, particularly since the rate rise, and dealers say speculative interest has centred on a depreciation around election time.
"All the bets are on the election day and after," said one, who declined to be named.
David Goone, senior vice president for marketing at the CME, said futures were strong and options hit record volumes.
"We are seeing a little more options volume in puts, which means people are hedging the chance of the peso going down," he added.
